en: Regarding the time when the *Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Sūtra* was difficult to hear, there is no sequence of priority or posteriority; by eliminating hearsay, it establishes the "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) mentioned above, hence it is called "at one time.
Such are the differing explanations. Next, to distinguish errors and non-errors, first the matter is verified through facts, and subsequently [scriptural authority] is cited.
As for the scriptural evidence and factual verification, how are they?
As it is said in the sutras:
Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment.
According to the Hīnayāna tradition, it was six or seven days after the Buddha had completed his realization that he began preaching the sūtras.
At that time, Ānanda was still in [the Buddha's] embrace;
his body did not participate in the assembly.
After the Buddha had attained enlightenment,
it was twenty years before [the youth] first left the household life,
and thirty years later he became an attendant.
From this point onward,
most of the various sūtras that have been explained were not heard directly from [the Buddha]. Although they were not heard directly, [they were nonetheless received].
Furthermore, the sūtras that have been compiled also state "at one time"; thus,
it is clearly known that there is such a thing as "one time."
This does not mean that [the account] is not authentic.
Furthermore, within the Hīnayāna,
one cannot say that Ānanda was a provisional manifestation.
On what basis can it be said that speaking and listening occur simultaneously?
Furthermore, humans are by nature subtle;
how then can it be known that Ānanda was born on the very night the Buddha attained the Way?
In the future, this will refute me.
To prove this point, one must understand the causal conditions for Ānanda’s establishment of his name.
Ānanda is a foreign term; in this [language], it means "Joy."
The designation [of these] is established based on three causes and conditions.
First is the past cause and condition,
as stated in the sūtras:
When Śākyamuni was practicing as a bodhisattva,
he was a potter named Mahāprabha.
In a past life, he encountered Śākyamuni Buddha;
his father was named Śuddhodana and his mother was named Māyā.
His attendant disciple was named Ānanda,
together with his retinue of followers.
Now there was no difference between them.
Thereupon, he made this vow:
"May I, in the future, attain the path of Buddhahood."
Just as the present Buddha did,
he has now attained Buddhahood by virtue of this original vow.
Therefore, the attendant now has the same name as before, Ānanda.
This is the second present causal condition.
The bhikṣu Ānanda was handsome in countenance; those among the people who saw him [were struck by his beauty].
There was no one who did not rejoice;
for this reason, he was named "Joyful.
Therefore, in the sutra:
Praise to Ānanda:
Your face is like the moon, your eyes are clear lotuses;
the ocean of the Buddha’s Dharma resides within the heart of Ānanda.
Third, his parents established his name.
For what reason did his parents give him the name "Joy" (Nanda)?
Because it arises at a time of joy.
What is this time of joy? It is the night when the Tathāgata attained the Way.
At the age of nineteen, the Tathāgata left the city.
Having gone forth, he practiced meditative concentration for five years.
For six years he starved himself until his body became extremely emaciated; the father-king sent men to constantly go and observe his meals.
Knowing that [life] is extremely frail and wasting away,
one should always fear that it will not last;
thus, the Bodhisattva acts at a later time.
Knowing that hunger was not the path,
he accepted the milk-rice with the desire to attain perfect enlightenment.
Māra then thought thus:
If the Buddha-way were accomplished,
my realm would be emptied;
yet I have heard that the Way has not yet been accomplished.
He shall surely frustrate their ambitions.
Thereupon, he led his officials and subordinates,
numbering one billion eight hundred million.
When those who possess the various requisites for awakening come seeking a bodhisattva,
the bodhisattva at that time enters the meditative concentration of supreme intention and loving-kindness.
He causes the retinue of Māra to fall into confusion and ruin.
Once Māra has been subdued,
he then thinks to himself:
"By the power of my great compassion, I can overcome the Bodhisattva;
I shall distress his father.
Having thus resolved, he proceeded to the palace of Śuddhodana.
He uttered these words:
"Prince Siddhārtha has passed away last night."
When the king heard this,
he fell from the grove;
after a long while, he finally regained consciousness.
He then lamented with grief, thinking:
"I had expected that my son, remaining at home, would become a Wheel-Turning King;
who would have anticipated that he would leave the household life and achieve nothing at all? Not long after this, [the son attained enlightenment].
The deity of the Bodhi tree attained accomplishment through the Buddha-way and further manifested celestial transformations.
Congratulations to the Father King.
When you attain Buddhahood,
the heavens shall rain down exquisite flowers.
Thus he made offerings;
for this reason, he was named King Keṅ (Joyful).
At that time, he also went up to the palace of Śuddhodana.
He spoke these words:
"Great King, you should know that this is Prince Bhūmideva."
Last night, when the morning star appeared,
he subdued the hosts of Māra's army and attained the Way of Buddhahood.
At that time, the king gave rise to doubt,
thinking: "Just now there was a deity who said, 'My son is dead.'"
Now there are others who say that you have attained the Way;
how can any of this be trusted?
The Bodhi deity said,
"My words are to be trusted;
that which occurred just now was Māra."
Therefore, I merely troubled you.
I am a tree spirit of the Bodhi tree;
it was beneath my tree that the Buddha attained the Way.
Therefore, they congratulated one another.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"My son is at home."
He was destined to be a Wheel-Turning King;
today he has left the household life to become the Great King of the Dharma-Wheel.
There is no contradiction between the two;
previously we heard that he was dead,
but now we suddenly hear that he is alive.
He was greatly delighted;
hearing further that the Way had been accomplished,
he was doubly and greatly delighted.
Not long thereafter, King’s younger brother, Droṇodana,
gave birth at night to Ānanda; having explained the significance of the birth, he was brought to the royal palace.
"Last night a son was born to me.
The King then replied,
"My son shall attain the Way."
You have given birth again to a son;
as all manner of celebrations gathered together,
he was given the name "Joy."
Based on this evidence, one can know with certainty that Ānanda was born on the night he attained the Way.
Since Ānanda was born on the night he attained the Way, [it follows that...]
On what basis can it be said that speaking and listening occur simultaneously?
The evidence of the matter is thus.
Next, I shall provide scriptural proof.
When the Buddha first attained enlightenment,
he was at the Deer Park of the Rishis in Vārāṇasī for the sake of the five bhikṣus.
The turning of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths is called the *Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma*.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...
The bhikṣu Ānanda previously compiled this sutra;
he was about to compile this sutra.
First, he ascended the high seat and spoke these verses himself:
"When the Buddha first preached the Dharma..."
At that time, I did not see it;
rather, I heard it passed down from one to another that the Buddha was traveling in Vārāṇasī.
For the assembly of five bhikṣus,
he turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; within that sūtra:
The Way has already been heard of;
it further speaks of "one time," making it clear that there is indeed one time.
This is not a phrase intended to exclude [certain] biographies;
the clarification of what is not [the case] is as follows.
Next, the correct meaning is revealed.
Regarding the term "at one time":
from the perspective of the Buddha's own explanation, it refers to the occasion for his transformation of beings.
Regarding the term "time" (kāla):
within the single lifetime of the Buddha,
the periods of his transformative activity were numerous.
To exclude other times,
the word "one" is used; that is,
the phrase "at one time."
It exists extensively within the sūtras,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"At one time, I..."
In the kingdom of Kāśī,
at one time, I was on the bank of the Gaṅgā River.
At one time, I was in the Śītavana charnel ground. At another time...
In Rājagṛha, there were not just one such occasion;
the expression "at one time" (ekasmin samaye) refers to this.
It is similar to that.
How is this known? Because at one time it followed from behind.
This does not belong to the preceding [section].
This is known by relying on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
At the beginning of the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it says:
"Thus have I heard at one time. Although the holy teachings are numerous, [this formula is used].
In brief, there are only two:
first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, which teaches the Dharma for śrāvakas.
That which is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
that which teaches the Dharma for bodhisattvas is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Within the *Ghoṣākośa*, there are two types of teachings:
first, the śrāvaka-śrāvaka;
second, the pratyekabuddha-śrāvaka.
As for the śrāvaka:
such a person has, from the beginning,
sought the path of the śrāvaka.
They contemplate the Four Noble Truths with joy and attain the nature of a śrāvaka; then,
in their final body, they reach liberation.
Encountering the Buddha as he wished to rest,
the Tathāgata preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him,
whereby he attained realization of the Way.
Originally possessing the nature of a śrāvaka,
they now hear the sound once more and thereby attain realization of the Way.
For this reason, they are called "śrāvakas of śrāvakas.
As the Sūtra says: "For those who seek the state of a śrāvaka, he taught the Four Noble Truths."
Based on this discourse,
those who are pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas are,
by their original nature, human beings.
They seek the path of the pratyekabuddha;
they constantly delight in contemplating the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination,
thereby perfecting the nature of a pratyekabuddha.
In his final body, he encountered a Buddha who taught him the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination,
whereby he attained realization of the path;
this was due to his original nature as a pratyekabuddha.
In their final body,
they awaken to the Way upon hearing a sound;
for this reason, they are called Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas.
The Sūtra states that for those who seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha,
the twelve links of dependent origination are taught;
it is based on this that the following is said.
Although these two differ,
they both aim for the same minor fruit;
they rely upon the teachings and occupy the same station.
For this reason, they are collectively designated as "śrāvakas" when contrasted with these two types of persons.
The Dharma that is taught is designated as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
the instructions therein are likewise twofold.
The first is gradual entry;
the second is sudden enlightenment.
As for what is called "gradual entry":
This person, in the past,
practiced the Great Dharma; midway through,
they heard and awakened to the Small [Vehicle].
Later, one returns to enter the Great [Vehicle].
Because the Great [Vehicle] comes from the Small, it is called "gradual.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Lesser Vehicle,
I now cause them as well to enter into this Dharma.
This refers to those who enter the bodhisattva path gradually.
As for those who speak of "sudden enlightenment," there are certain sentient beings.
Having long cultivated roots of goodness associated with the Mahāyāna,
they now first behold the Buddha and are immediately able to enter the Great Vehicle.
The great does not arise from the small;
this is designated as "sudden.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
There may be sentient beings who,
from lifetime to lifetime since time immemorial,
have constantly received my transformation.
Upon first seeing my body and hearing what I say,
they all immediately believe and accept it.
Entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata is sudden enlightenment;
entering gradually is that of the Bodhisattva.
Relying on shallow stages to reach the distant goal,
the Bodhisattva of Sudden Enlightenment transcends them all at once to realize the Great [Truth].
Although the sudden and gradual approaches differ,
because the recipients of the Great [Vehicle] at that time were of one accord,
[the teaching] was presented to these two types of individuals accordingly.
As for what has been taught:
although the noble teachings of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka are numerous,
they do not transcend these [categories].
Therefore, Nāgārjuna said:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
Kāśyapa and Ānanda..."
In the city of Rājagṛha,
the Three Piṭakas were compiled as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
Mañjuśrī and Ānanda were at Mount Cakravāḍa,
where they compiled the Mahāyāna.
It constitutes the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
The *Bhūmivastu* also states:
"The Buddha [taught] for the sake of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas."
He practiced the path leading out of suffering and preached the sūtras;
he was the one who compiled the scriptures.
These are compiled into two collections: those that explain the practices of the śrāvakas constitute the Śrāvaka-piṭaka,
while those that explain the practices of bodhisattvas constitute the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
It constitutes the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Furthermore, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"The twelve divisions of the scriptures."
Only the Vaipulya section constitutes the Bodhisattva-piṭaka;
the remaining eleven sections do not.
This is the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
therefore, one should know that within the Noble Teachings there is nothing that transcends these two.
These two are also called the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna,
or the Half-Teaching and the Full-Teaching;
though their names have been altered, [the essence remains].
The meaning is not different.
As for this present sutra,
among the two baskets (piṭaka), it belongs to...
It is subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka;
it is the wheel of Dharma of the sudden teaching for those whose faculties are matured.
Having already understood the scope of the teaching,
we shall next explain its title.
That which is now called "The Buddha-Spoken Benevolent Kings' Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā" is as follows:
"Kai" (蓋) is an alternative name for the *Piṭaka* (Basket).
The reason why the title of every sūtra is placed at its beginning is to seek the Dharma that it elucidates.
This sutra takes true nature as its central tenet;
therefore, it is presented at the very beginning.
However, the establishment [of tenets] in various sutras differs.
There are many such types;
some are named according to their subject matter,
such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and so forth.
Sometimes it is named after a person,
such as Sāha, Śuśadatta, and so forth; sometimes it is established as a designation based on its function, such as "the scale."
As in the *Śuṣkavṛkṣa-sūtra* and others;
or names derived from metaphors for hindrances,
such as the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, and so forth.
Alternatively, it may refer to the simultaneous obstruction of both person and phenomena,
as in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and other texts; or it may refer to the subsumption of phenomena under the category of "factual reality."
For instance, in texts such as the *Vaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, there may be titles consisting solely of the Dharma or the metaphor,
as in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and others; or there may be titles where both the person and the subject matter are established together.
There are many such instances, as in the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-vyādhi-sūtra* and others.
As for this present sutra:
The person and the dharma constitute the name;
that which the Tathāgata has spoken is the name of this person.
"Prajñāpāramitā" is the name of this Dharma. The Dharma relies upon persons for its transmission.

Therefore, one must understand the methods for the *pārivāsika* (one under probation) and the *mānāpya* (one undergoing penance). These are the methods required for the formal acts (*karmas*), which appear at the beginning of various sūtras.
Regarding individuals, there are four types.
First, the person who speaks is identified,
such as Śrīmālā and others.
Second, the person who asks the question is introduced.
First, as in the *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-sūtra* and others;
second, as in the *Śānti-putra-sūtra* (The Story of Śyāmaka) and others; third, as in the *Sahantana-sūtra* and others, which cite what was taught.
Fourth, those who were converted,
such as the woman Sumati in the *Yuyao jing* (Sūtra of the Jade Bracelet) and others;
now, those by whom [the teachings] were spoken are cited.
There are five different types of speakers.
The first is the Buddha’s own teaching.
Second, the teachings spoken by noble disciples;
third, the teachings spoken by devas;
fourth, the teachings spoken by ṛṣis and others.
The Fifth Discourse on Transformations.
This sutra was spoken by a noble disciple of the Tathāgata.
Completed transcription on the second day of the sixth month in the nineteenth year of the Kaihuang era.
